[s1]
Driving through northern Orlando on Orange Blossom Trail used to smell
amazing.
Not “that’s nice” amazing.
[/s1]

[s1]
Not perfume amazing.
It was thick, warm, and sweet in a way that didn’t stay politely in your
nose.
[/s1]

[s1]
It landed right on the tip of your tongue, like your brain was
half-convinced you were tasting something.
You’d roll the window down a little more without even thinking about it,
[/s1]

[s1]
because Florida was announcing itself.
And back then, Orange Blossom Trail wasn’t ironic.
It earned the name.
[pause]
[/s1]

[s1]
When I was younger, Florida citrus wasn’t a niche industry or a branding
exercise.
It was everywhere.
[/s1]

[s1]
Groves stretched to the horizon.
Roadside stands weren’t novelty stops — they were destinations.
Not little shelters with a cash box, but full family-day places: gift shops,
[/s1]

[s1]
samples, candy counters, play areas.
Places where you’d leave with a bag of oranges and something you didn’t plan
on buying… but bought anyway.
[pause]
[/s1]

[s1]
And today, you can still see the buildings — empty, too specific to reuse,
too big to ignore.
Like abandoned stage sets from a play Florida no longer performs.
[/s1]

[s1]
Florida citrus didn’t start small.
Commercial production took off after the Civil War, railroads connected the
state to northern markets, the soil cooperated, and the climate mostly
[/s1]

[s1]
behaved.
By the late 1800s, Florida was already producing millions of boxes a year.
Yes, freezes wiped things out more than once — the Great Freeze of the 1890s
[/s1]

[s1]
nearly erased the industry.
But citrus didn’t die.
It adapted.
[/s1]

[s1]
Growers moved south.
[/s1]

[s1]
They replanted.
They rebuilt.
That rhythm — adapt, move, rebuild — defined Florida citrus for more than a
[/s1]

[s1]
century.
By the mid-20th century, Florida citrus wasn’t just agriculture.
It was identity.
[/s1]

[s1]
After World War II, frozen concentrate and refrigerated trucking turned
orange juice into a national habit.
Breakfast in America came with a glass of Florida OJ.
[/s1]

[s1]
Florida grew so dominant that orange juice futures literally became a movie
plot.
That’s Trading Places.
[/s1]

[s1]
At its peak, Florida was producing nearly 300 million boxes a year.
If Florida had been its own country, it would have ranked among the world’s
top citrus producers.
[/s1]

[s1]
And yes — there was a rivalry: Florida versus California.
Florida was juice.
California was fresh fruit.
[/s1]

[s1]
Different climates.
Different strengths.
For decades, Florida wore the crown — not because California was weak, but
[/s1]

[s1]
because Florida was massive, efficient, and relentless.
Then came people.
As Florida’s population exploded, groves turned into subdivisions and
[/s1]

[s1]
shopping centers.
Farmland became some of the most valuable real estate in the country.
Quietly, without a single dramatic event, the most profitable crop in
[/s1]

[s1]
Florida stopped being oranges.
It became houses.
This wasn’t betrayal.
[/s1]

[s1]
It was math.
[/s1]

[s1]
Weather has always been Florida citrus’s oldest enemy.
Freezes in the 1980s pushed growers even farther south — often into marginal
land, more exposed to storms.
[/s1]

[s1]
Then came the hurricanes.
Irma in 2017 tore through groves just as fruit was ripening.
Ian in 2022 delivered another blow.
[/s1]

[s1]
Entire seasons lost.
But weather still wasn’t the killer.
It was the setup.
[/s1]

[s1]
The real knockout punch came from something you can barely see: citrus
greening disease.
First detected in Florida in 2005.
[/s1]

[s1]
Spread by a tiny insect.
No cure.
No quick fix.
[/s1]

[s1]
Trees weaken.
[/s1]

[s1]
Fruit turns bitter and misshapen.
Yields collapse slowly, season after season.
Growers didn’t give up.
[/s1]

[s1]
They spent more.
Worked harder.
Bought time.
[/s1]

[s1]
But the rules had changed.
[pause]
[/s1]

[s1]
The numbers are staggering.
Florida citrus production dropped from about 300 million boxes to barely
15–20 million in two decades.
[/s1]

[s1]
That’s more than a 90% collapse.
Acreage fell by nearly two-thirds.
Packing plants closed.
[/s1]

[s1]
Jobs disappeared.
Entire supply chains evaporated.
Florida didn’t lose the rivalry to California.
[/s1]

[s1]
It was squeezed out by disease, weather, economics, and development — all at
once.
And the loss wasn’t just economic.
[/s1]

[s1]
It was cultural.
Place names still tell the story: Citrus County, Orange City, Winter Garden,
Frostproof.
[/s1]

[s1]
Even our license plate still carries an orange — a symbol of something that
barely exists in the landscape anymore.
You can still drive past the Citrus Tower.
[/s1]

[s1]
Same tower.
Different world below it.
So here’s the question that hangs over all of this — the one everybody asks
[/s1]

[s1]
sooner or later.
Will Florida citrus ever come back?
And the honest answer is… yes.
[/s1]

[s1]
Just not like that.
Smaller.
More technical.
[/s1]

[s1]
More local.
The old industry was built on scale: endless groves, mass production,
[/s1]

[s1]
momentum.
That world is gone.
Once groves are paved, they don’t come back.
[/s1]

[s1]
But survival doesn’t always look like resurrection.
Sometimes it looks like reinvention.
Today, the fight isn’t happening in endless fields.
[/s1]

[s1]
It’s happening in labs, in greenhouses, and in nurseries.
Researchers are developing greening-tolerant rootstocks.
Growers are testing protective systems.
[/s1]

[s1]
Others are shifting to specialty citrus and agritourism — smaller operations
built for resilience, not volume.
Florida citrus won’t be the giant it once was.
[/s1]

[s1]
But it doesn’t have to disappear.
And every now and then, on a warm day, windows down… [reflective pause]
I swear my brain still expects that smell on Orange Blossom Trail.
[pause]
[/s1]

[s1]
You can’t Google what a place used to smell like.
You either remember it… or you don’t.
And if you do, you know exactly what I’m talking about.
[reflective pause]
[/s1]
